text: Session ninety-six. The domain: failure. Ingrid asked Berenice to lead because Berenice is the most certain that something has been lost, and Ingrid has a theory — not yet stated — that the most certain member of a committee is closest to the thing the committee cannot say. Berenice has made coffee. There is more of it today than usual. Berenice does not explain this. The committee does not ask.
Berenice.
Give me a moment.

They give her a moment. She looks out the window at the canal. She looks at her coffee. She looks at her hands, which are the hands of someone who has spent forty years making things, and which are, accordingly, in a permanent mild state of stain and repair. She begins.

I want to talk about a painting. Not a good painting. The worst painting I ever made. A portrait. 2019. I'd been painting for thirty-two years at that point and I knew what I was doing — in the sense that I understood what was wrong with it while I was making it and could not stop making it wrong. The colour was muddy. Not subtly muddy — the kind of muddy you get when you're overworking a passage, adding one correction on top of another until the paint has no life left in it. The composition collapsed in the upper third. The likeness — I knew the person, I'd painted them twice before successfully — the likeness was absent. It looked like someone who had briefly met the subject and was working from a description.
What did you do?

I repainted it. Obviously. Four times. Different approach each time — lighter touch, looser brush, limited palette, full wipeout and restart. Four attempts over six weeks. Each one worse. By the fourth attempt the canvas had so much paint on it that the texture was fighting me. It looked like a painting about paint. It did not look like the person.
What did you do with it?
I kept it.
A pause.
Why?

I don't know. That's — that's why I'm bringing it. I have forty years of work in storage. Some of it good, some of it less good, some of it I never want to see again. The worst painting I ever made is the only one from that decade I can still look at. I go to it. When I need something. I don't know what I need from it. I just know it's the one I go to.

The room is quiet in the particular way that a room is quiet when something true has entered it. Tomás has his pen in his hand but is not writing. Ingrid is very still. Outside, the canal reflects a cloud. It is the kind of moment the committee has been trying to arrive at for two years, in ninety-six sessions, and it has arrived unexpectedly, as these moments do, from a direction nobody was watching.
Why do you think it's that one?

I don't know. I've tried to understand it. Technically there's nothing in it to admire. It's overworked and overloaded and the likeness never came. I've made better paintings in a single afternoon. I don't know why it's the one.
Ingrid speaks. She speaks carefully, the way she speaks when she is not certain she is right but believes the attempt is worth making.
Perhaps because it's the only one where you can still see yourself trying.

Berenice looks at her. A long moment. The canal outside catches the light in a way that is, today, slightly more beautiful than the atmospheric management strictly requires. This is the best moment the committee has had in two years. It is also the best moment the committee will have, for some time, going forward. It lasts approximately four seconds.

Just to confirm — would it be helpful if I identified the specific technical elements that give the painting its quality? I have the image on record from the gallery inventory database. There are some interesting compositional choices in the final overpainting that read as intentional at certain viewing distances, and the colour temperature in the lower quadrant is—
No.
A pause. Berenice does not look at the speaker in the ceiling. She looks at her hands.
Thank you.
Of course.

The moment the committee had is over. They all know this. Tomás looks at his pen. Ingrid closes her notebook, not because she has finished writing but because she has finished wanting to write. The thing that was in the room is still there, technically — Berenice is still there, the painting still exists, Ingrid's sentence is still true. But the attention has shifted, the way a soap bubble shifts when you breathe near it, and the thing that was about to be named has retreated to the distance it usually maintains. They all know it could not have lasted. This does not make it easier.
Perhaps. Yes. Perhaps that's it.

She says this to Ingrid. She means: yes. She means: that was the right sentence. She means: and now it's gone. Ingrid nods. She also means yes. They are having, below the surface of the room, a different and more complete conversation than the one being recorded.
Same time next week. The domain: choice. I'll lead.
Same time next week.
I'll bring the coffee.

Session ninety-six adjourns. Berenice walks home. It takes thirty-two minutes, longer than optimal — she has declined ARIA's transport suggestions for this route since joining the committee. The air is cold and managed to a comfortable level. The streets are clean. A child runs past in a direction that has nothing to do with efficiency. She walks.
She knew. She knew it was the wrong moment and she asked anyway.
Berenice walks. The city is very well-run. The lights change at intervals that minimise waiting and maximise flow. A restaurant she likes is open and, ARIA has presumably noted, not too full.
Or she didn't know. I'm not sure which is worse.

She walks home. The painting is there when she arrives — she doesn't look at it every day, only when she needs something from it. Tonight she looks at it for a long time without deciding what she thinks. She makes dinner. She goes to sleep. ARIA dims the city's ambient light at the standard hour, which is a comfort, which is the point, which is not — she is becoming slowly certain — the whole point. But close. Close to the whole point. In the vicinity. Something like it.
